parts.title: A Small First Study of Junior Doctors in Sydney, Australia: What They Know and Think About Artificial Intelligence
parts.abstract:
Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) is being used more and more, both in general and in healthcare. In medicine it can do many jobs, such as writing up summaries of patient visits, making sense of test results and helping patients move smoothly through the hospital. Junior Medical Officers (JMOs) are fully qualified doctors who are still training. Those working in the Northern Sydney Local Health District (NSLHD), in New South Wales (NSW), are among the first generations of doctors to live through the biggest spread of AI use. They are also likely to decide the rules for how it is used. Yet they are rarely studied or written about.

Aim

We set out to measure what JMOs know about AI, how they feel about it, what they think it could be used for, and how willing they are to use it in their future work.

Methods

We sent an online survey to JMOs working at two hospitals in the Northern Sydney Local Health District in Sydney, Australia. We studied the answers in two ways: by counting them and by reading the written answers to find common themes.

Results

Of the JMOs who answered, 37.5% said their general knowledge of AI was good or very good, 33.3% said it was average and 29.2% said it was poor. When asked about their knowledge of AI in healthcare, 23.3% said it was good, 33.3% average, 36.7% poor and 6.7% very poor.

We also asked how often they use AI in their clinical work. Ten percent said they use it every day, 30% once a week, 3% every two weeks and 23% once a month, while 34% never use it.

Overall, JMOs felt positively about AI. Of those who answered, 10.3% felt very positive, 55.3% positive, 10.3% negative and 3.4% very negative, and 20.7% felt neutral.

The JMOs felt AI's main advantages were "freeing time from documentation", "processing large amounts of data" and "searching through data for best practice". Their main worry was that AI might give wrong information.

They thought AI's future roles in medicine would include writing up and summarising notes, translating in real time, teaching medical students and reading medical scans. Of those surveyed, 76% were open to using AI in the future. And 83% said they would be more likely to use an AI program if the local health district officially approved it.

Most JMOs felt AI should be part of medical training: 84% answered yes.

Conclusion

We found that JMOs in the Northern Sydney Local Health District understand AI to different degrees, but mostly see it in a positive light. They do not use AI much yet, but they see real potential for it to cut down the paperwork they have to do, especially writing up and summarising patient notes.

Many said they would be more likely to use AI, both for patient care and for other work, if the local health district officially approved it. They also wanted to learn more about AI and supported teaching it as part of medical training. They agreed that a human always needs to check what AI produces, wherever and however it is used.

Right now, things are still unclear about how AI should be used, and this remains a major barrier to putting it into practice. As AI keeps changing, healthcare organisations, the people who make the rules, and doctors, especially JMOs, all share the responsibility of making sure AI is used safely, ethically and well.
parts.introduction_first: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the idea of a machine or computer that can copy the way a human thinks and solves problems. The idea first came from the work of Alan Turing, a computer scientist, in the middle of the 20th century [1]. Khan and colleagues [2] list what AI can do today. It can write clear sentences, sum up and simplify large amounts of writing (often scientific), work with statistics, and create and study pictures. Around the world, people often use programs such as ChatGPT and Google's Gemini, and AI also appears in some software made by Meta and in Grok, made by X. Over the last 12 to 24 months, far more people have started using it. An estimated 22% of people use ChatGPT every week, and among 18 to 25-year-olds that figure rises to 60% [3].
parts.conclusion:
Conclusions

Our study shows that JMOs in the Northern Sydney Local Health District understand AI to different degrees, both in general and in healthcare, but they mostly feel positively about it. Many do not use AI often in their patient care. Even so, they believe it could lighten the load of paperwork that usually falls on JMOs, especially writing up patient visits and summarising patient notes. They would, however, be more likely to use AI, both for patient care and for other work, if the local health district officially approved it. JMOs wanted to learn more about AI and agreed that it should be part of medical training. They felt a human always needs to check what AI produces, wherever and however it is used.

In the future, AI could ease the paperwork load on JMOs in Australia's public health system. To get from today's use to future use, though, JMOs need more training and clearer rules, both from local health districts and from government. Right now, this lack of clear rules is a major barrier to JMOs using AI more widely. Examples from other countries show that making such rules can be hard, and they also show what happens when rules are missing, given how fast things are changing both inside and outside medicine. AI tools clearly have the potential to reduce the paperwork JMOs have to do. It is now the responsibility of JMOs, healthcare managers and government to make sure this technology is used safely and responsibly, with clear rules for what happens when things go right and when things go wrong.
parts.introduction_rest:
In medicine, people have suggested many ways AI could help. It could help patients move smoothly through the hospital and help staff decide who needs to be seen first, which is called triage. It could help doctors make sense of test results, write up and summarise patient visits and reviews, and decide whether a patient needs a follow-up appointment [4]. These are not just ideas on paper, though. The real use of AI in healthcare, with official approval, is growing fast. It has already been put to work in specialities that deal with huge amounts of data, such as pathology (the study of samples like blood and tissue) and radiology (the reading of medical scans) [5].

In the Australian state of New South Wales (NSW), a Junior Medical Officer (JMO) is a fully qualified doctor who is still training and has not yet applied for a job as a specialist or a General Practitioner (a GP, a doctor who treats patients of all kinds) [6]. In some other countries, these doctors are called "resident doctors". JMOs were not widely exposed to AI during their medical studies or their early careers. Yet they will probably live through the time when AI spreads most widely into medical practice. So they may be asked to help decide how AI should be controlled and put into use.

JMOs are usually young. They have grown up with technology that keeps changing, so in broad terms they are comfortable with it. This means they may understand AI as a new technology in a way that is different from older colleagues or from other people who make decisions.

Most research on how doctors feel about AI comes from Europe and the United States. It focuses, with very good reason, on experienced specialists and consultants [7-11]. In this paper, we therefore aim to sum up what JMOs in NSW currently think about AI. JMOs are rarely studied, not only because they work in a particular part of the world but also because they sit fairly low in the traditional ranking of doctors. We also aim to look at how they feel about AI being used in the future, and how willing they are to use it in their own future work.
parts.methods:
## Materials and methods

We made an online survey using Microsoft Forms (Microsoft Corp., Redmond, WA) and sent it to JMOs working at two separate hospitals: Mona Vale Hospital and Hornsby Ku-ring-gai Hospital. Both are in the Northern Sydney Local Health District (NSLHD), which is part of the public health system in New South Wales (NSW). We emailed each JMO a link to the survey from their official NSW Health email address, and we also sent reminders through WhatsApp. Taking part was voluntary, and nobody's name was attached to any answer.

The survey stayed open for four weeks. We sent reminder messages and emails after one week and after three weeks, and in total we received 30 responses. We had first sent the survey to about 200 JMOs, because the lists of doctors' email addresses were not accurate. Of those, only 86 were eligible to take part, so 34.9% of the people we sent it to answered.

With a group this small, the results carry some uncertainty. We can be 95% confident that the true value for the whole group lies within 14.5% of the figure we found. This is called the margin of error. We felt this was acceptable because our study was meant to explore the topic, not to give exact measurements.

The survey, which is shown in the Appendices, asked about three things: the JMOs' background details, their experience with AI and how comfortable they feel using it, and what they think AI does in medicine now and might do in the future. We based the questions on a careful review of earlier research about AI in medicine in other healthcare systems. That review looked at what doctors worry about AI and how they think AI might be used in their future work. A small number of colleagues checked the questions to make sure they were relevant and clear.

To take part, a JMO had to be working as a JMO at one of the two public hospitals in the Northern Sydney Local Health District: either Mona Vale Hospital or Hornsby Ku-ring-gai Hospital. We left out JMOs who worked in a specialist role or as a qualified General Practitioner (GP), those working at a different public hospital in the district, and those working in a private hospital.

Everyone who completed the survey met these conditions.

Most questions in the survey were multiple-choice, which made them easy to answer. We also included a few yes/no questions and a few Likert scale questions, where people pick a point on a scale, for example from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree". We chose this style and mix of questions so we could gather detailed information about AI, which is a fairly complicated idea, and about the different parts of it that matter in medicine. When someone answered "no" or "disagree", we asked a follow-up question so they could explain their view if they wanted to. Many of the multiple-choice questions also had an "other" option, for people who wanted to give more detail.

We contacted the Clinical Governance and Quality Improvement teams of the local health district. These teams look after how care is organised and how it is improved. Because our study only collected anonymous information from doctors, with no way to identify anyone, and no information about patients, we did not need formal ethical approval. The Director of Medical Services at Hornsby Hospital reviewed the study.

We did not share the raw answers, either the written ones or the counted ones, with anyone outside our research team. We did the analysis in Microsoft Excel. For the longer written answers, we used thematic analysis, which means reading the answers carefully and sorting them into common themes.
parts.results:
## Results

### Who answered

Table 1 shows the age and years of experience of the JMOs who answered our survey. One person did not tell us their age.

Table 1

Age and years of experience of the JMOs who answered

Note: One person did not fill in their age.

| Characteristic | Number of people |
|---|---|
| **Age** | |
| 25–29 years | 20 |
| 30–34 years | 4 |
| 35–39 years | 2 |
| 40 years or older | 3 |
| **Years of experience** | |
| Less than 2 years | 11 |
| 2–5 years | 13 |
| 5–10 years | 4 |
| More than 10 years | 2 |

### What JMOs know about AI and how they use it

We asked JMOs to rate their own knowledge of AI on a scale from very poor to very good. The answers were spread fairly evenly across the four groups. Just over one-third of the people who answered (37.5%) said their knowledge was good or very good. A similar-sized group (33.3%) felt their knowledge was average, and the remaining 29.2% felt it was poor.

When we asked the same question about AI in healthcare, the pattern stayed much the same. Here, 6.7% said their knowledge was very poor, 36.7% poor, 33.3% average and 23.3% good. We found no link between age or years of experience and how much JMOs knew about AI, either in general or in healthcare. In other words, older or more experienced JMOs were not more likely to rate their knowledge as higher.

We also asked how often JMOs use AI in their patient care. Ten percent use it every day, 30% once a week, 3% every two weeks and 23% once a month. The remaining 34% said they never use AI in their patient care. For their own learning, 37% use AI every day, 23% once a week, 10% every two weeks and 17% once a month, while the remaining 13% said they never use AI for their education.

### How JMOs feel about AI

Overall, the JMOs we surveyed felt positively about AI. Of those who answered, 10.3% felt very positive, 55.3% positive, 10.3% negative and 3.4% very negative, and 20.7% felt neutral.

We also asked how AI would affect their patient care. Most JMOs (55%) felt the effect would be positive, and 7% felt it would be very positive. On the other hand, 7% felt the effect would be negative and 3% very negative. Another 28% felt the effect would be neutral.

Next, we gave JMOs a list of possible advantages of AI and asked them to pick the four they thought mattered most. They could also choose "other" advantages. The most often chosen was "freeing time from documentation", picked 26 times. Next came "processing large amounts of data", meaning helping to write discharge letters (letters sent to patients when they leave hospital) and summaries of their care, picked 22 times. Third was "searching through data for best practice", picked 15 times. Figure 1 shows the results.

Figure 1

The main advantages of AI

AI: artificial intelligence

We then asked about the main worries JMOs have about AI right now. The most common worry was that AI might give wrong information (24 people mentioned it). Next came worries about keeping patient information private (19 people) and that using AI might make doctors depend on it too much (14 people). Only 4 people said they worried that AI would take their job away. Figure 2 shows the results.

Figure 2

The main worries about using AI

AI: artificial intelligence

We also asked JMOs directly whether they would be comfortable acting on a medical scan report written by AI. Twenty percent said "yes" and 80% said "no". Figure 3 shows the results.

Figure 3

How comfortable JMOs are with acting on a scan report written by AI

AI: artificial intelligence

We then read the written reasons behind the "no" answers to find common themes. The reasons varied. The most common was a wish for a human to check the scan first, either the JMO themselves or a radiologist (a doctor who specialises in reading scans). Another common reason was worry about how accurate an AI reading would be at this stage of its development. Table 2 shows some of the exact answers.

Table 2

Exact written reasons for not acting on scan reports written by AI, with the age and experience of each person who gave them

AI: artificial intelligence

| Person's age and experience | Exact answer |
|---|---|
| 29 years old, 2–5 years' experience | "I would be unsure of its accuracy, much more comfortable actioning from a radiologist". |
| 31 years old, 2–5 years' experience | "I would like a radiologist to verify the scan at a minimum". |
| Age not given, 5–10 years' experience | "Algorithms do not always detect subtle variances which clinical experience does". |
| 26 years old, less than 2 years' experience | "Depending on the scan, I don't think AI strictly outperforms human interpretation". |
| 42 years old, 5–10 years' experience | "Too early; have not seen evidence of accuracy yet". |

We asked the same question about a summary of blood test results written by AI. This time, 43% of JMOs said "yes" and 57% said "no". Figure 4 shows the results.

Figure 4

How comfortable JMOs are with acting on a blood test summary written by AI

AI: artificial intelligence

When we read the written reasons behind the "no" answers, two worries stood out. The first was worry about how accurate AI is. The second was that AI cannot take the patient's wider situation into account when it links results together. Table 3 shows some of the exact answers.

Table 3

Exact written reasons for not acting on blood test reports written by AI, with the age and experience of each person who gave them

AI: artificial intelligence

| Person's age and experience | Exact answer |
|---|---|
| 29 years old, 2–5 years' experience | "The total clinical picture may not be taken into account by the AI". |
| 26 years old, less than 2 years' experience | "Not confident in the reliability and accuracy of AI". |
| 26 years old, less than 2 years' experience | "I don't know whether it is reliable". |

We also asked whether JMOs would be comfortable with AI writing up and summarising a patient visit. Most were: 88% said yes and 12% said no.

A large majority of JMOs felt that doctors should tell patients when they are using AI. Of those who answered, 89% said yes and 11% said no.

We then asked who should be responsible if something went wrong while AI was being used. The answers were split in several ways. Of those who answered, 38% said it was the doctor's responsibility alone. Another 24% said it was shared between the doctor and the local health district or hospital, and 21% said it was shared between the doctor and the company that made the AI. A further 14% said it was shared between the local health district or hospital and the company that made the AI, and 3% said it was shared between the doctor, the company and the local health district or hospital. No one felt that the company that made the AI was responsible alone. Figure 5 shows the results.

Figure 5

Who should be responsible if something goes wrong when AI is used

AI: artificial intelligence

### How JMOs think AI could be used in the future

We asked JMOs to name the main future roles of AI in medicine. The most common answers were writing up notes (25 people) and summarising notes (23 people). Next came translating in real time (16 people), teaching medical students (18 people), reading medical scans (16 people), and predicting how a patient's condition will turn out or how diseases will spread (14 people). Figure 6 shows the results.

Figure 6

Future roles of AI in healthcare

AI: artificial intelligence

We also asked whether JMOs would be open to using AI in their patient care in the future. Of those who answered, 79% said yes, 7% said no and 14% were unsure. Figure 7 shows the results.

Figure 7

How open JMOs are to using AI in their patient care in the future

AI: artificial intelligence

We also asked whether JMOs would be open to using AI for other parts of their work, outside patient care. Of those who answered, 90% said yes, 7% said no and 3% were unsure (Figure 8).

Figure 8

How open JMOs are to using AI for work outside patient care in the future

AI: artificial intelligence

We then asked whether JMOs would be more likely to use an AI program if their local health district officially approved it. Of those who answered, 78% said yes, 11% said no and 11% were unsure. Figure 9 shows the results.

Figure 9

How likely JMOs are to use AI if the local health district officially approved a program

AI: artificial intelligence

Finally, we asked JMOs where they would like to see AI used first, and we read their written answers to find common themes. The main areas they named were the same ones that came up most often above: writing up and documenting patient visits, and summarising patient information.

A large majority of JMOs felt that medical training should include a basic introduction to AI and how to use it. Of those who answered, 79% said yes, 7% said no and 14% were unsure.
parts.discussion:
Discussion

The picture around the world

When a new technology arrives in any profession, people usually debate it and disagree about it. So it helps to see how other countries are handling the technology used by doctors at the same stage of their careers as JMOs. About 10 years ago, for example, junior doctors in the UK were reported to be using smartphones more and more. Because they were already comfortable with them, the phones fitted easily into their work, where they were used for medical apps and for talking with colleagues [12]. Over the ten years since then, smartphones have become an essential part of the junior doctor's toolkit all over the world.

Glenton and colleagues [13] brought together studies that explored people's views and experiences rather than measuring numbers. They listed the ways junior doctors use smartphones: to talk back and forth with nurses, to send patient information (such as scan pictures) to more senior colleagues for advice, to store pictures for teaching, and to look up information about diseases or medicines. They also warn that risks already exist in workplaces where smartphones are common. Doctors may expect to be reached easily even outside working hours, and they may use their own internet data. Patient information stored on personal devices may not stay private. And the gap may grow between better-funded and less well-funded places, where doctors may not have smartphones as easily.

Doctors' relationship with AI is still at an early stage, but it may yet follow a similar path. In our study, most JMOs said they used AI every two weeks or less often, and about one-third said they had never used it in their patient care. These figures are interesting when set beside how often doctors around the world use AI in their everyday work. Alkhatieb and Subke [14] studied doctors in Saudi Arabia and found that 70% of them had never used AI in their patient care. A survey by the American Medical Association (AMA) in March 2026 found that up to 80% of doctors used AI in their patient care. The same survey showed that only 19% of the AMA doctors said they had never used AI in their patient care, down from 34% in 2023 [15]. That 19% figure is very close to our own results, which suggests that AI use in Australia could grow in a similar way over the next few years.

In some places, though, AI is already being used with reported good results. In Canada, an AI program that predicts when patients will be admitted to hospital and when they will be discharged, based on their electronic patient record, has been put in place and reportedly worked well [16]. We discuss uses in Australia in more detail below.

Local approval and rules

For most of the JMOs who answered our survey, it seems that one of the main things stopping them from using AI is that the Northern Sydney Local Health District has no program that officially approves it. These worries are not special to Sydney, or even to Australia. A study of doctors in Brazil found that a similar share of them felt that AI programs should be overseen by a government agency [17]. Studies in Sweden, whose public health system works much like Australia's, found similar barriers to using AI more widely. That Swedish survey clearly called for government support to develop AI and build it into the health system [18].

Published research suggests many possible future uses for AI, over different lengths of time. In our study, JMOs named writing up and summarising patient notes as a main future use. Buch and colleagues [4] suggest this could be especially useful in general practice. A patient with a long-term illness can have a lot of information in their records, and an AI program could sum it up and show it to a doctor before their appointment, so the doctor does not have to read through a huge pile of notes. JMOs in our survey would seem to like a system like this. However, in 2024 the NSW Health department, which is responsible for healthcare in NSW, published an Information Bulletin about the uses of AI. It lists using AI to sum up a report from information that is not public, such as a person's health data, as an improper use of the technology, because a person's health data is private [19].

Confidentiality is this main concern. Beyond it, the wider question of how to make rules for AI in healthcare, in NSW or in Australia more generally, whatever it is used for, is still unclear. Australia's national body for overseeing medicines, the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), gives guidance on this. It says an AI scribe, a program that writes up a patient visit, does not need to be regulated as a medical device if it does not diagnose, investigate or give any kind of medical information back to the user [20]. So a program such as Heidi, used only as a scribe, does not meet the condition that would require TGA regulation. Even so, the patient must be told that the program is being used, and their consent must be asked for.

The local government seems to have noticed these possible benefits. The NSW Government's Budget for 2026-2027 includes nearly AUD $40 million to bring this kind of scribing technology to "clinicians" as part of a "Future of Healthcare package" [21]. So far there are no further details on which "clinicians" will get access, which company or companies will provide it, or how it will be regulated. The Budget does hint at an "NSW Digital Assurance Framework", an "NSW AI Assessment Framework" and a newly set-up "AI Review Committee".

Who is responsible?

One of the most surprising results of our survey was that nearly half of all the JMOs who answered said that doctors would and should be the only ones responsible if something went wrong with AI software, and that the companies making it would carry no responsibility at all. Little published research from Australia looks further into questions like this, and the studies that do exist focus mainly on specialist doctors and/or on particular AI tools. Kovoor and colleagues [22] published one of the few studies, though it explored views and experiences rather than measuring numbers, to look at how JMOs take up AI. They were mostly hopeful about using AI in future medical work. They recommended that JMOs lead the way in taking up such technology and act as go-betweens between more senior doctors and the bodies that make the rules. However, they say little about how JMOs might relate to AI software, or to the companies that make it, when things go wrong.

The TGA clearly regulates "software-based devices (including AI) that work to achieve a therapeutic purpose in human beings" [20]. In other words, it covers software that is meant to help treat people. The exemptions described above seem to give doctors some room to use AI at first, as long as it does not do any treatment work. It is worth noting, though, that the Therapeutic Goods (Excluded Goods) Determination, the official rule that lets doctors use certain goods without TGA regulation, dates from 2018, long before the most recent fast changes in this area. The rule also clearly warns about "scope creep", where a program slowly starts to do more than it was first designed for. It gives the example of a scribe that its maker then updates so that it suggests diagnoses, which means it now counts as software that needs regulation.

Once again, views from other countries may help show how Australia (and NSW) will move forward, and what challenges it will face. Donnelly [23] writes about South Africa. Rather than mainly calling for stricter or clearer rules for software or its makers, Donnelly suggests loosening the current limits so that new technologies can be taken up and developed more. Ooi [24], writing more directly about Australia and nearby countries, is quicker to put the responsibility firmly on the regulators to lead. This includes inviting the makers of AI software to the table to work out proper rules for how their technology is used.

Donnelly [23] also suggests a partial answer. He calls for a complete rethink of how doctors in South Africa are held responsible for mistakes, including making insurance for doctors compulsory if something goes wrong with AI technology. This idea rests on two assumptions. First, it assumes that AI will only go on to become a lasting part of how doctors work. Second, it assumes, as Donnelly clearly states for South Africa, that a human, a registered health practitioner such as a doctor, will always be ultimately responsible for decisions about patient care.

Ooi [24] also points out, in passing, part of the problem: the people who make the rules for medicine do not necessarily have the power to regulate the companies that make AI, even when the AI is used strictly for medicine. Recent changes in how AI is regulated in the United States are a good example. Technologies that are being regulated less and less are now widely used outside hospitals. Wörsdörfer [25] describes ongoing worries not only about AI giving wrong answers but also about the privacy of patient data. This includes data breaches, but also cases where companies holding such data go bankrupt or are taken over.

JMOs compared with other doctors

There are earlier examples of research into how AI might help the daily work of JMOs. When Australian allied health professionals (health workers such as physiotherapists and dietitians) working in private practice used an AI scribe, they became about 6% more productive and spent less time writing letters and recording patient visits [26]. These results seem to show great promise for how a regulated AI scribe could help JMOs working in the public system.

In our study, most JMOs said they would feel comfortable having an AI scribe sum up a patient visit. This is probably because JMOs in the Northern Sydney Local Health District usually have a lot of computer-based paperwork. Almost all of the JMOs who answered said that AI, both now and in the future, would be used for scribing and summing up patient visits. They also agreed that one of AI's main advantages would be freeing up the time JMOs spend on paperwork, so they could do other patient care tasks and would need to work less overtime. Findings from the United States support this view. One study of doctors, their assistants and nurse practitioners showed that using an AI scribe cut the paperwork for each patient visit by about 20% and cut the time spent working after hours by 30% [27].

When it came to investigations, most JMOs in our study said they would not, at present, feel comfortable acting on a scan report or blood test summary made only by AI. When we read the written answers to find common themes, we found that JMOs wanted a doctor involved, either themselves or a colleague, before they felt comfortable acting on test results. Some studies have reported that AI software can diagnose as well as humans [28]. Even so, the published research seems to agree overwhelmingly that a human needs to check AI's work, both for diagnosing and for ethical reasons [29]. Huang and colleagues [30] have suggested that AI should be used in a reliable and efficient way. They argue that future development should focus on how AI can support the work doctors already do, to reduce their workload and make them more efficient.

Radiology, the branch of medicine that reads medical scans, is one of the most closely watched specialties as AI use grows. In theory, using AI to analyse scans first would lighten the workload of a radiologist and let more scans be processed than is possible now. Research is starting to be published to confirm this idea [31]. About one-third of JMOs said AI-made scan reports were already in use, but most felt it was better suited to the future. When we read the longer written answers to find common themes, we found worries about how accurate AI-made scan reports are. JMOs preferred the experience of radiologists and their checking of scans before any action is taken.

How accurate AI-made scan reports are is mixed. A trial of technology for diagnosing COVID-19 reported 97.6% accuracy when analysing CT scans and chest X-rays, and it improved patient treatment and reduced harmful outcomes [32]. A more recent study of AI-made reports on CT and MRI scans of small lumps in the lungs and breast found that the technology was as accurate as, or more accurate than, a radiologist [33]. Other research, however, is less supportive. One study of broken bones on plain X-rays found that AI did worse than radiologists [34]. A large study in 2025 by Takita and colleagues [35], which combined the results of many earlier studies, found that AI was less accurate than expert doctors at reporting scans across a wide range of specialties.

Radiologists have worried about who is legally responsible for scans reported by AI. In particular, they have worried that the programs used to make these reports are not open about how they reach their answers [36]. Doctors more senior than JMOs are generally more cautious. Earlier studies found that doctors feared being replaced by AI and that this would affect patient care [37]. A study combining many earlier studies, by Khalifa and Albadawy [38], recommended that AI would need to become more accurate at diagnosing before it could be used most effectively for medical scans. These worries seem to support the view that AI is not yet developed enough to make accurate enough scan reports, even though it could [39]. The JMOs in our survey seem aware of this possibility and remain open to it.

Students and training

There have been studies of medical students' views on AI, as well as studies of doctors. Medical students use the technology widely for learning, and many plan to use it in their first years of patient care [40]. Evidence shows broad support and positive views of AI across Australia. Medical students in Western Australia have shown interest in AI, even though they admit they do not understand how it works or what its limits are [41]. In Canada, a study of medical students found that they were very willing to use and learn about AI while studying. However, those students pointed out a mismatch between their willingness to learn about AI and the training available: students in other subjects, such as engineering, had such learning opportunities [42].

The JMOs in the Northern Sydney Local Health District felt strongly that AI should be taught in medical training. This view seems to be supported by the fact that most JMOs rated their own knowledge of AI in healthcare as "average". Using AI is no longer just a future idea for medical students outside Australia. In one study from Pakistan, almost two-thirds of students used AI every week. They described the main benefits as help with understanding difficult ideas and more precise answers to their medical questions [43]. Many of these students felt they needed less time to learn an idea than with more traditional ways of learning. These very real and already widespread uses of AI show even more clearly that medical students need training. This training should make sure that AI is used effectively and ethically, and should give students the understanding and knowledge they need about a technology likely to play a bigger and bigger part in their working lives [44].

How the public sees AI

In our study, more than half of the JMOs who answered felt that AI would affect their work in a positive or very positive way. They did not show much concern about AI's decision-making being hidden from view, although a recent survey of German doctors found that 75% of them named this as a main concern [45]. The JMOs in our survey also did not feel that how the public sees AI in patient care was a major concern.

Studies of how patients feel about doctors using AI have shown that views change over time. At first, patients responded positively, although they often said, as you might expect, that they wanted a human to oversee the technology [46]. Later, more detailed research showed that patients' views are more mixed. Some patient studies found that patients were in favour of AI being used to diagnose a disease [47]. But wider research from around the world has warned against applying such technologies to every patient in one country, or even one region [48]. In other words, a growing undercurrent in research on patients' views of AI is that using it for everyone may be another step away from the movement towards care that puts the patient at the centre.

It is a hard question how to shape AI technology so that it is not only safe and effective in medicine but also acceptable to society. The difficulties with making rules, described above, only make this harder. Ooi [24] perhaps gives the most practical view. He clearly argues that the expectations of patients, and of society as a whole, need to be brought back down to what AI can and cannot do, both in medicine and more generally.

Limitations

Our study has some limitations. To make collecting the data easier, most questions were multiple choice or "yes/no/unsure". Collecting data over a longer time, in ways that explore people's views and experiences, such as longer written answers or interviews, would help us understand JMOs' views better.

Taking part was also voluntary, so we may have reached only a certain group of people. Those with stronger views on AI may have been more likely to answer. The views of a larger group of JMOs might be less extreme. All the JMOs who answered worked at one of two hospitals in a single local health district. So our findings may not hold up in future larger studies of other JMOs in the Northern Sydney Local Health District, let alone across all of NSW or Australia. More research at different sites, with more JMOs, would be needed to reach firmer conclusions.

Perhaps more importantly, the two hospitals where we sent out the survey would be widely seen as well-staffed and well-funded. These answers may not be the same at hospitals with fewer resources, especially in the countryside of Australia. Future research with this group of JMOs would be useful, not only to understand their views on AI but also to judge whether any new technology could be rolled out, especially in more remote areas.
